title: Warfarin, sip two C nine, V K O R C one and sip four F two

segs.text: Section twenty. Warfarin and its three genes. Warfarin is an anticoagulant: it lowers the number of working clotting factors. Clotting factors are proteins first made in an inactive form. An enzyme called gamma glutamyl carboxylase, G G C X, turns them into active clotting factors.
G G C X cannot do this alone. It needs reduced vitamin K, the active form of vitamin K. No active vitamin K, no active clotting factors.
Each time G G C X uses active vitamin K, the vitamin K becomes vitamin K epoxide, which G G C X cannot use. The epoxide must be converted back before it can be used again.
The enzyme that converts the epoxide back to active vitamin K is vitamin K epoxide reductase. Its gene is V K O R C one, and this enzyme is warfarin's target.

Warfarin is a mixture of two forms, R warfarin and S warfarin, and both block V K O R C one. With it blocked, the epoxide is not converted back, active vitamin K runs short, and G G C X cannot make active clotting factors. That is how warfarin works, and why vitamin K is the antidote in a warfarin overdose.
S warfarin has most of the activity, three to five times more potent than R. sip two C nine clears S warfarin into inactive metabolites. R warfarin is weak and is cleared by several sip enzymes.
The third gene, sip four F two, breaks down active vitamin K and removes it from the cycle. It acts on vitamin K, the antidote, not on warfarin.

A gene that changes how fast a drug is cleared is a pharmacokinetic gene; two C nine is one. Its variants star two and star three lower activity, star three the most, but do not remove it. S warfarin is cleared more slowly, so the same dose builds up higher and bleeding risk rises. These patients need a lower dose.

A gene for the drug's target is a pharmacodynamic gene; V K O R C one is one. Some V K O R C one variants have low activity, and a less active target needs less drug to block it, so the dose is again lower.

Four F two goes the other way. With low activity, less active vitamin K is broken down, so more of the antidote is on board, and the patient needs more warfarin, not less. A more active four F two works the other way.

A patient can carry low activity variants in both the target and the clearing enzyme; she called this a double whammy. No variants in either gene: about five milligrams of warfarin a day. Two C nine star three star three, both copies star three, with no V K O R C one variant: less. Two variant copies of V K O R C one plus two C nine star three star three: the lowest dose, to avoid bleeding. Body weight and gender also affect the dose.
